---
title: "Quiz: superpixels"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** Name two reasons to segment superpixels instead of pixels, and the main risk.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Size of the graph; what happens to a missed boundary?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reasons: a much smaller graph (hundreds of nodes instead of tens of thousands, so graph cuts, walkers and hierarchies are cheap), and regions on which features (means, histograms, texture) are more stable than on single pixels. Risk: a boundary that no superpixel follows is lost for every later step.
:::

---

**Q2.** SLIC with $N = 65\,536$ pixels and $K = 1024$ superpixels: what is the grid spacing $S$, and the size of each centre's search window?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$S = \sqrt{N/K}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$S = \sqrt{64} = 8$ pixels; each centre searches a $2S \times 2S = 16 \times 16$ window.
:::

---

**Q3.** What happens to SLIC superpixels when you increase the compactness $m$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which term of $D^2$ grows?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The position term $(m\,d_s/S)^2$ dominates: superpixels become more regular (near-squares on a grid) and follow colour edges less; weak edges are ignored. Small $m$ gives ragged superpixels that follow every edge and texture.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does SLIC need a connectivity clean-up after k-means?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does the distance $D$ know anything about connectedness?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each pixel is assigned to its nearest centre independently; nothing forces the pixels of one label to touch each other. With noise or small $m$ a label can be scattered into fragments. The clean-up keeps each label's largest piece and gives the orphan pieces to a neighbouring superpixel.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why is SLIC's cost per iteration independent of $K$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many windows cover a pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Windows of side $2S$ on a grid of spacing $S$ overlap so that each pixel lies in about 4 of them, whatever $K$ is. So each iteration computes about $4N$ distances, while plain k-means computes $NK$.
:::

---

**Q6.** The achievable segmentation accuracy of a set of superpixels is 0.97. A classifier labels the superpixels and reaches a pixel accuracy of 0.96. Could a better classifier reach 0.99?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does "achievable" mean here?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. Any method that gives each superpixel one label is at most 0.97 accurate (the majority label of every superpixel). To do better you need finer or better superpixels, or a pixel-level method.
:::

---

**Q7.** Superpixels with high boundary recall but a high under-segmentation error: how is that possible?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Recall checks true boundaries; the error checks superpixels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Boundary recall only asks whether every true boundary has a superpixel boundary nearby. Very many, ragged superpixel boundaries achieve that easily, even if some superpixels still spill across a true boundary somewhere else (counted by the under-segmentation error). Both measures are needed (and ragged boundaries also lower boundary precision).
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Show that, for fixed assignments, moving a SLIC centre to the mean of its pixels (in colour and position) minimises the cluster's sum of $D^2$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$D^2$ is a weighted sum of squares.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\sum_p D^2(p, \mathbf c) = \sum_p \lVert\mathbf f_p - \mathbf f\rVert^2 + \frac{m^2}{S^2}\sum_p\lVert\mathbf x_p - \mathbf x\rVert^2$, with $\mathbf c = (\mathbf f, \mathbf x)$. The two parts depend on separate coordinates; each is a convex quadratic minimised where its gradient vanishes: $\sum_p(\mathbf f_p - \mathbf f) = 0$ and $\sum_p(\mathbf x_p - \mathbf x) = 0$, i.e. at the means. The weight $m^2/S^2$ does not move the minimum.
:::
